author: Unknown Author
text:
Most AI failures in Pharma happen before a single line of code is written.
 
It is not the model. It is not the infrastructure. It is not the vendor.
 
It is what happens, or fails to happen, in the weeks before kickoff.
 
After supporting AI initiatives across Life Sciences, the same pattern keeps repeating. The pilots that stall share five upstream failures, long before the first commit.
 
1. The use case is defined without a value hypothesis.
"An AI project for MSLs" or "a copilot for medical writing" is launched with no clarity on which decision improves, how much that improvement is worth, and how it will be measured. Without a hypothesis, there is no way to know whether the pilot worked.
 
2. The data is not where it is assumed to be.
HCP master data fragmented across markets. Clinical, commercial, medical and RWD sitting in silos that do not interoperate. No clear ownership of data quality. The AI team discovers in week 3 that preparing a clean, consented dataset will take months, not days.
 
3. No one has decided who owns the outcome.
Who funds it? Who builds it? Who runs it in production? Who answers to a regulator if something goes wrong? Without those four answers in writing, the pilot moves through no-man's land until something breaks.
 
4. Compliance enters at the end, not the beginning.
GxP validation adapted to AI/ML, EU AI Act, FDA guidance, privacy, human-in-the-loop. When these requirements arrive at validation stage, the model has to be redesigned. When they enter the initial design, they save months.
 
5. There is no stop-rule.
Teams agree on how to start, not on how to stop. Pilots that are not working stay alive on political inertia, consuming talent and budget that should be on the use cases that actually move the needle.
 
The useful question is not "which model should we use?".
 
It is this one: can we put on the table the value hypothesis, the outcome owner, the data map, the regulatory frame, and the stop-rule, before an engineer opens a notebook?
 
If the answer is yes, the pilot has a real chance.
 
If the answer is no, the model will be the least of your problems.

author: Ebelechukwu Lucy Okafor
text:
AWS vs. GCP for a cloud-native startup,  a DevOps Engineer's honest take:

❖ Cost: Both offer generous free tiers. GCP's sustained-use discounts apply automatically, with no commitment. AWS requires Reserved Instance purchases or Savings Plans to unlock equivalent savings.

❖ Ecosystem: AWS has the widest service catalogue and the largest talent pool globally. GCP leads on Kubernetes,  Google invented it,  and on BigQuery for data-heavy workloads. If your architecture is Kubernetes-first, GCP feels native in a way AWS doesn't.

❖ Turnaround: Both can be production-ready in days with Terraform. The real differentiator is what your team already knows and what your workload actually demands.

My recommendation after working across all three clouds:

For most startups,  AWS offers the widest support, the largest community, and the most hiring options. Go GCP if your architecture is Kubernetes-first or ML-heavy. Consider Azure if your business is already deep in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The best cloud is the one your team can operate confidently at 2 AM when something breaks.
Which cloud are you running in production right now, and would you make the same choice again? 


Ebelechukwu Lucy Okafor · Cloud & DevOps Engineer · Lagos, Nigeria · AWS | GCP | Azure | Terraform

text:
Why your data frames are loose 

The function df.merge is used to combine two or more data frames. These could be related... data frames relating data.

Most of the times they are, or data frames that have columns you need.

But they are separate, scattered even.

Bringing them together as one data frame is df.merge( )'s specialty.

Remember to save the merged data frame with a new name. 

ALWAYS ‼️

How this goes beyond data analysis?

For every model you build, you need data, and that data isn't one place. 

It's usually in bits and parts. scattered all around your workflow. 

Using the function df. merge. 

It helps you gather your data like a broom sweeping together dust particles or more like saying gathering the building blocks of a lego sets to build, say, a LEGO city block, LEGO battle ship, or even a NINJAGO LEGO set.

 This is something that not just analysts, but also AI engineers, ML engineers, and even probably data engineers use when building databases and models and getting the insights from scattered messy data. 

It doesn't matter how good your data is. If you don't know how to bring it together for your analysis or model — it's going to show.

And that's something you would not want your boss to find out about 😂. 

As an analyst moving toward AI engineering, df.merge() isn't just a pandas function — it's how I'm learning to think like an engineer.

Day 19 of #90DaysOfPython

Save this for when your DataFrames start running away from each other. 😂

 PS: when using df.merge( ) do you just combine random columns or do you combine columns specific to what you need?

author: Rajeev Chachra, open to work
text:
The anomalous correlations that define the Indian Software Industry - insights from anecdotal exchanges with 1000 plus candidates 

·     There is a poor correlation between skill and pay

·      There is a poor correlation between years of experience and skill

·      There is a poor correlation between resume and actual work

·      There is a poor correlation between designation and responsibility

·      There is a poor correlation between leadership position and vision

·      There is an unsaid belief that upselling and what is the best for the customer are one and the same

·       There is an unsaid belief that good project management is more crucial than technical implementation (including architecture, tech stack as these have lower status)

·       There is an unsaid belief that those who get started quicker are smarter and more productive (never mind the rework)

·       There is an unsaid belief that those who sound more authoritative are more knowledgeable

·       There is an unsaid belief that all new technologies are superior to older ones

·      There is an unsaid belief that two cheaper resources are better than one excellent but expensive resource.

·      There is an unsaid belief that LinkedIn recommendations are a true measure of capability

·      There is an unsaid belief that premier institute candidates are better than others - always

·      There is an unsaid belief that the one who speaks first in the meeting is definitely leadership material

·      There is an unsaid belief that the one who asks and verifies requirements before starting is slow and “doesn’t get it”.

·      There is an unsaid belief that resumes must be tailored to address the job description irrespective of one’s experience.

·      There is an unsaid belief no matter how varied, extensive, demanding a job description might be, hiring someone who does not have all the skills is not acceptable

I moved to India 4 years back after working in the US for 22 years mainly as a software professional in varying roles from individual contributor as a developer to technical lead to client facing engagements to architecting solutions, project management etc. In these last 4 years I have interviewed more than 1000 candidates from freshers to VP of Engineering including AI engineers, ML Ops, full stack, backend, frontend, vibe coders etc working mainly as a technical skills screener. I admit that these insights have been gleaned from my anecdotal exchanges with the candidates and are not the result of any extended study or survey. 

I find these insights rather alarming especially as the global software landscape is becoming more competitive and perhaps India’s only true moat of wage arbitrage can only take it so far. Unless the industry acknowledges these trends and takes pro-active, conscious decisions to change course, the future may be bleaker than what we expect. 
Apologies if I have hurt any sentiments but I believe this deserves a thought.

author: Nandini raj, open to work
text:
The hidden challenge of Generative AI is that the model itself is often the simplest part to handle.

Anyone can integrate an LLM API in a single afternoon and create a polished prototype. However, when attempting to scale that demo for real enterprise users, issues like latency spikes and skyrocketing costs can arise, leading to system failures without robust infrastructure.

Interestingly, I learned how to address these challenges before I ever worked with an LLM.

My initial experience in cloud development involved tasks like mapping contact flows, writing serverless Lambdas, and debugging in CloudWatch dashboards. This foundational work taught me how enterprise systems function.

Over the past 4.5 years, I transitioned from managing cloud infrastructure to developing GenAI systems that operate on it. Tools like AWS Bedrock, LangChain, LangGraph, and vector databases became essential in my daily work - not just for creating impressive demos, but for delivering production-grade AI that positively impacts business metrics.

I focus on the outcomes when real users interact with the system, rather than proof-of-concepts that merely exist in presentations. For instance, when tasked with creating an enterprise RAG platform, we engineered a solution that reduced query-resolution latency by 98%, transforming it from minutes to sub-seconds. Also implemented token-level streaming with FastAPI for a seamless experience and automated the source-to-vector ingestion pipeline to eliminate manual efforts.

This is the type of GenAI work I am passionate about: identifying friction points, automating repetitive tasks, and building an LLM layer that operates effectively at scale. Whether it’s creating an automated complaint-letter engine that reduces manual drafting by 95% or integrating an LLM-as-a-judge layer for audit readiness, my focus is on production.

Due to my extensive experience in this field, I have begun teaching. In the past year, I have trained and up-skilled over 21,000 students and working professionals in applied ML and Generative AI. Teaching complex orchestration frameworks to engineers has deepened my understanding of my own technology stack.

Now, I am seeking my next challenge.

I am open to new opportunities and looking for a full-time role as a Generative AI Engineer or Machine Learning Engineer, where I can develop, scale, and deliver impactful AI systems.

If you are building an AI team, scaling production RAG or agentic workflows, or need someone who can bridge the gap between raw ML and enterprise product deployments, let’s connect.

Feel free to DM me or contact me at nandini.raj03112000@gmail.com.

(If your network is hiring, a share or tag would be greatly appreciated!)

author: Hamza Suleiman
text:
UK startups raised €14.8bn in the first half of 2026, up 102% on H1 2025 (HSBC Innovation Banking UK / Dealroom, 10 July). AI took €11bn of that more than four times last year.

Reads like a hiring boom. 

68% went to late stage companies, up from 42% a year ago. Isomorphic Labs, Nscale, Wayve and Ineffable Intelligence pulled in around €5.5bn between four firms.

The capital is real, but it's pooling at the top. If you're hiring mid or senior ML engineers at a growth stage company, you're bidding for the same people those four are paying to lock up.

author: Bobby Kamal
text:
Healthtech AI has a branding problem: every headline is either "AI will save billions" or "AI is making things worse."

I think there's another conversation to be had.

Healthtech is one of the corners of AI right now where the engineering has to be as rigorous as the ambition. $4B went into digital health in Q1, the strongest quarter since the pandemic. Lilly signed a $2.75B deal for AI-discovered drug candidates. You don't put that kind of money behind a drug discovery platform unless it actually works in production.

And the sector isn't taking that on faith. Roughly 200 U.S. state bills are being tracked around AI in healthcare this year, several of them zeroing in on one specific question: can a person double-check this before it affects someone's care? It's the industry holding itself to a standard many AI products never have to meet.

Which is exactly why I think it's one of the most underrated places to build right now. You don't get to ship fast and fix it later. You have to design for trust from day one, for the clinician who'll actually use it and the regulator who'll actually read the audit log.

If you're an ML/AI engineer who wants to build something that has to hold up outside a demo, in front of a clinician and a regulator, healthtech is where that muscle gets built.

author: Nitesh Agarwal (He/Him)
text:
An average AI query uses about 30 ml of water, while a single piece of steak requires 4,663 litres. 🥩

That comparison is the whole argument in this article by Ana Lúcia Castro, Devoteam Product Owner. The internet circulates numbers about AI's water footprint, and the figures tell a slightly different story.

Ana breaks down where that water actually goes (data centre cooling, the electricity generation behind it, the difference between Scope 1 and Scope 2 consumption) and stacks it against things nobody thinks twice about.

A one-hour Zoom call costs more water than 50 AI prompts. Ten minutes of 4K video costs more than a full day of typical AI use.

It's not an argument that AI is water-free. Data centres are real infrastructure with a real footprint, and the piece covers what AWS, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA are each doing to engineer that down.

But the framing matters. If you're worried about your water footprint, the shower is a better place to start than the search bar.

author: Unknown Author
text:
Two years ago, "knowing AI" meant you could call an API and write a decent prompt. That bar is gone.

The engineers getting hired and trusted with production systems in 2026 are not the ones who know the most models. They are the ones who understand the system around the model.

After 6+ years shipping these systems, here is the mental map I would hand anyone starting today. 17 concepts, 5 layers.
1- The retrieval layer (1 to 3)
Embedding models, vector databases, RAG. Still, the foundation of almost everything. Most "AI features" in production are retrieval problems wearing an LLM costume.

2- The efficiency layer (4 to 7)
Context engineering, semantic caching, model routing, and AI gateways. This is where the cost and latency battles are won. Nobody notices this layer until the invoice arrives.

3- The action layer (8 to 11)
Function calling, tool use, MCP, and external integrations. The difference between a chatbot that describes work and a system that does it. MCP has quietly become the standard wiring here.

4- The agent layer (12 to 14)
Agent harness, execution loops, memory systems. Where most teams are right now, and where most of the hard, unsolved problems live.

5- The trust layer (15 to 17)
Guardrails, observability, evaluations. The least glamorous layer and the one that decides whether your system survives contact with real users.
The uncomfortable truth: most engineers are strong in one or two layers and hand-wave the rest. The retrieval people ignore evals. The agent people ignore the cost. The infra people ignore what the model outputs. The rare skill in 2026 is knowing how all 17 connect and where your system will break first.

That last part is the actual job. Every broken AI system that lands on my desk fails at a layer boundary: a solid RAG pipeline with no evals, a capable agent with no cost controls. When you carry the full map, diagnosis is fast. That is why we can usually tell a client where their system is bleeding within the first call, before writing a single line of code.

I am Muhammad Ghulam Jillani, Founder and Lead AI Engineer at Jillani SofTech, Top Rated Plus on Upwork. We have delivered 22+ production AI systems across healthcare, finance, legal, and SaaS: agentic RAG platforms, autonomous agents, LLM products, and traditional ML, where it beats GenAI. Real numbers: 91% factual accuracy on a clinical decision support system, 8,000+ daily queries on an enterprise knowledge assistant, 900+ daily workflow triggers on a revenue automation.

Save this as your checklist. Audit your system against all 17 before your users do it for you.

Which layer is your weakest right now?

author: Maitreyee Mulay, open to work
text:
🤖 AI isn't replacing engineers. It's changing what they spend their time on.

Here's how AI is showing up in cloud environments right now.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔍 Smarter monitoring
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

AWS CloudWatch anomaly detection uses ML to learn what normal looks like for each metric and flags deviations automatically.

Instead of setting static thresholds that generate false positives, the model adjusts to seasonal patterns, traffic spikes, and deployment cycles.

Less alert fatigue. Faster detection of genuine issues.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🛡️ Automated security
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

AWS GuardDuty uses ML to continuously analyse CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs for suspicious behaviour.

AWS Macie uses ML to automatically discover and classify sensitive data sitting in S3 buckets.

These aren't rule-based systems. They learn. They catch things that no predefined rule would catch.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💬 AI-assisted development
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Amazon CodeWhisperer generates code suggestions directly in the IDE, trained on AWS APIs and best practices.

AWS Bedrock gives developers access to foundation models from Anthropic, Meta, and others to build generative AI applications on top of AWS infrastructure.

Cloud engineers are now building products with AI baked in, not just deploying infrastructure underneath it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📊 AI for cost optimisation
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

AWS Compute Optimizer uses ML to analyse actual resource utilisation and recommend right-sized instance types.

AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to identify unexpected spend patterns before they compound.

AI is turning cost management from a monthly review into a continuous automated process.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💡 The shift
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The engineers who thrive are the ones who understand what AI is doing underneath and can build, configure, and debug the systems that run it.

AI doesn't replace cloud expertise. It raises the baseline for what cloud expertise means.

The companies moving fastest are not hiring one “AI person.”
 
They are building an AI operating model.
 
The source post called out a hard problem:
 
94% of CEOs say AI skills are priority #1.
 
90% of enterprises still cannot find enough AI talent.
 
That gap creates a practical question for leaders:
 
Which AI roles do we actually need first?
 
→ Management roles set direction.
 
✅ Chief AI Officer owns AI strategy, governance, and executive accountability.
 
✅ Head of Applied AI turns use cases into production outcomes.
 
✅ AI Product Manager manages the AI product lifecycle end to end.
 
✅ Responsible AI Lead reduces deployment risk before trust problems scale.
 
✅ Director of AI Transformation connects roadmap, delivery teams, and change management.

✅ AI Application Developer integrates AI into business software.
 
✅ AI Redteam Engineer tests model weakness before customers or regulators find it.
 
✅ Data Engineer keeps the pipelines reliable enough for AI to work.
 
→ Business roles turn AI into operating leverage.
 
✅ AI Accounting Analyst improves forecasting, reconciliation, and reporting workflows.
 
✅ AI-Powered Auditor detects anomalies, fraud signals, and control weaknesses.
 
✅ AI Compliance Analyst monitors regulations and flags AI-driven risk.
 
✅ AI HR Data Analyst converts workforce data into better people decisions.
 
✅ AI Customer Success Manager uses AI insights to predict churn and improve adoption.
 
The diagnostic is simple:
 
If AI is still “owned by IT,” you probably have a strategy gap.
 
If experiments do not reach production, you probably have a delivery gap.
 
If teams cannot trust outputs, you probably have a governance gap.
 
If business units do not use the tools, you probably have an adoption gap.
 
AI hiring is shifting from isolated specialists to connected role families.
 
Leaders who map the gaps now will move faster later.
 
The question is not “who can prompt?”
 
It is “who owns strategy, delivery, risk, and adoption?”
 
Which role is missing from your AI roadmap right now?

author: Daniel Kornaś
text:
Building audio generation systems often means stitching together separate codebases for speech, singing, conversion, vocoders, and evaluation.

Amphion is an audio, music, and speech generation toolkit for researchers and engineers exploring generative audio.

It helps you study and build multiple audio workflows through task-specific recipes, model implementations, preprocessing tools, visualizations, and evaluation metrics.

Key features:
• Speech synthesis – recipes and implementations include FastSpeech2, VITS, VALL-E, NaturalSpeech2, and MaskGCT.
• Voice workflows – supports voice conversion, accent conversion, and singing voice conversion.
• Text-to-audio – includes a latent-diffusion recipe and implementation linked to the AUDIT research.
• Evaluation toolkit – covers pitch, energy, intelligibility, spectral distortion, and speaker-similarity metrics.
• Learning and setup – provides model visualizations plus Conda and GPU-enabled Docker installation paths.

It’s open-source (MIT license).

author: Samuel Nnadi
text:
The 2 AM Page That Didn’t Happen.

It’s the middle of the night. Your production database spikes to 99% CPU utilization.
Normally, the story goes like this:
The static alert triggers.
The on-call engineer wakes up in a cold sweat.
They spend 45 minutes digging through raw logs, trying to figure out if it’s a heavy database query, an active connection leak, or just expected nightly traffic.

Meanwhile, the user experience degrades, and the business bleeds trust.
But what if the system could diagnose, analyze, and heal itself before the engineer's alarm even goes off?

That’s the exact problem I wanted to solve.

I’ve been building a secure, automated AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) Self-Healing Pipeline on AWS using Terraform. Instead of relying on rigid, manual thresholds that cause alert fatigue, this architecture uses Machine Learning to take matters into its own hands:

🔹 ML-Driven Telemetry: Dynamic CloudWatch Anomaly Detection monitors our EC2 & RDS resource usage, mapping mathematical bands to traffic patterns rather than arbitrary percentages. 

🔹 Root-Cause Analysis: Integrated Amazon DevOps Guru watches our resource telemetry, automatically isolating deep system bottlenecks (like a runaway process or a connection leak). 

🔹 Closed-Loop Remediation: An EventBridge pattern routes the AI's diagnostic insights to an AWS Lambda function, automatically executing AWS Systems Manager (SSM) runbooks to safely reboot the affected service daemon, instantly restoring baseline metrics.

The result? The system detects the anomaly, isolates the root cause, triggers a self-healing script, and logs the entire incident, all while the engineering team is fast asleep.

We shouldn't just be building architectures that run; we should be building architectures that think.

I've documented the complete infrastructure code and bootstrap modules in my latest repository.

text:
The reality of running a business in the summer holidays...

Yesterday I spent the day in the Pyrenees with my son, racing go karts down ski slopes and making the most of the school holidays.

At the same time, the business didn't stop.
Between runs, I was scheduling final f2f interviews in Philadelphia for a Founding AE role with an exciting healthcare startup, signing terms with a new AI MedTech client in London, and submitting an ML Engineer for another live search.

People often assume founders either switch off completely or work around the clock.
The reality is somewhere in the middle.

You learn to make every hour count. Early mornings. Evenings. A few emails while waiting for your next run down the mountain. Then the mobile goes away and you're back to being Dad.

One of the reasons I started Octopus Search was to build something that gave me that flexibility. Not less commitment to my clients, but more control over how I deliver for them.

The work still gets done.
Candidates are still interviewed.
Clients are still supported.

But I also get to create memories with my son that won't come around again.
For me, that's what building a business is really about.

text:
Inside My Python Portfolio Backtester (Math + Engineering)

PROJECT CODE LINK: https://lnkd.in/dfhescMP

If a backtester leaks tomorrow’s data into today’s signals, you aren't trading—you’re hallucinating. Here is how I forced my pipeline to stay honest.

My portfolio engine is only as useful as its constraints. Here is the raw architecture and the mathematical boundaries I engineered into the Python pipeline.

Core pipeline:
- Data ingestion: Pulls OHLCV data from market sources into a clean, tabular format.
- Feature engineering: Computes momentum and volatility indicators, including log returns and Bollinger Band-derived features.
- Execution loop: A daily chronological loop tracking cash reserves, position sizing, trade counts, and commission friction so every trade flows through the same rules.
- Risk math: Applies standard formulations to the resulting P&L series, including Sharpe Ratio and strict peak-to-trough drawdown calculations

Two non-negotiable design choices:
- Chronological splits only: I strictly split train/test based on time. No random shuffling. No leaking the future into the past.
- Isolated scaling: All data normalization is fit solely on the training period and applied downstream. The model never peeks at future averages.

Mathematical assertions (my reality checks):
- Portfolio value cannot drop below zero.
- Maximum drawdown math must perfectly match manual edge-case arrays.
- Available cash limits must be respected on every execution order.

FinMind is being built for retail investors. If my internal engines cheat, the entire product is compromised. This architecture proves the math line by line before anything touches a user-facing tool.

author: Adedoyin Adeyemi
text:
🚨 PROMPT ENGINEERING IS NO LONGER ENOUGH.

The engineers building the best AI systems have quietly shifted their focus to something far more important:

👉 Context Engineering.

The difference between an AI assistant that sounds smart and one that actually solves problems is rarely the model.

It's the context you provide.

Think about it:

❌ Same LLM
❌ Same temperature
❌ Same prompt

Yet one response is generic, hallucinates, and misses the mark...

While another is precise, grounded, and production-ready.

The difference? Context

Here's a simple way to think about it:

> LLM = Brain 🧠
> Context = Environment 🌍

A brilliant brain without the right environment still makes poor decisions.


📌 The Context Engineering Checklist

✅ Define the objective clearly
✅ Give the model the right role and constraints
✅ Supply relevant knowledge—not everything
✅ Include examples when appropriate
✅ Structure information logically
✅ Use tools and RAG for external knowledge
✅ Leverage memory where continuity matters
✅ Continuously evaluate and refine



A MINDSET SHIFT:

❌ Don't ask:

> "How can I write a better prompt?"

✅ Ask:

> "How can I give the model everything it needs to succeed—and nothing it doesn't?"

That single shift can dramatically improve:

🎯 Accuracy
⚡ Reliability
💰 Token efficiency
🛡️ Hallucination reduction
🤖 Agent performance


I've put together this "Context Engineering Cheat Sheet" as a practical reference for AI Engineers, ML Engineers, LLM Developers, and anyone building AI agents.

📥 Save it.
🔁 Repost it so your network can benefit.
💬 And tell me in the comments:

What's the biggest mistake people make when working with LLMs?

Mine?

➡️ Treating prompts as magic instead of treating context as infrastructure.

Let's discuss. 👇

author: Santhosh kanna
text:
🚀 AI Knowledge Series #2 | RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which One Should You Choose?
One of the most common questions in the GenAI world is:
"Should I use RAG or Fine-Tuning for my AI application?"
The answer depends on the problem you're solving.
📚 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Think of RAG as giving your LLM access to an up-to-date knowledge library.
✅ No model retraining required
 ✅ Retrieves relevant information from enterprise documents in real time
 ✅ Lower implementation cost and faster deployment
 ✅ Easy to keep knowledge current
 ✅ Best for internal chatbots, document search, customer support, and knowledge assistants
🧠 Fine-Tuning
Fine-tuning teaches a model new behaviors by training it on domain-specific data.
✅ Improves performance for specialized tasks
 ✅ Adapts the model to your business language and workflows
 ✅ Better for structured outputs and domain-specific reasoning
 ⚠️ Requires training data, compute resources, and ongoing maintenance
Ideal for:
Medical AI
Legal AI
Code generation
Financial risk analysis
Highly specialized enterprise applications
💡 When should you choose each?
Choose RAG if:
Your information changes frequently.
You want quick implementation.
You need your AI to reference company documents.
You want lower infrastructure costs.
Choose Fine-Tuning if:
You need the model to learn a new behavior.
Your outputs require a consistent style or format.
You're solving a highly specialized domain problem.
Accuracy depends on adapting the model itself.
🔥 Pro Tip
The most successful enterprise AI solutions today combine RAG + Fine-Tuning:
Fine-Tuning for domain expertise and behavior.
RAG for real-time, up-to-date enterprise knowledge.
This hybrid approach is increasingly becoming the standard for production-grade GenAI systems.

author: Ashish Singh
text:
Ever feel like the tech world is a treadmill that speeds up every time you blink? 🤯 Especially in web development and AI, the sheer volume of new frameworks, libraries, and tools can feel daunting for aspiring developers like myself. It's easy to fall into the trap of "shiny object syndrome," constantly jumping to the next big thing without truly mastering anything.

What I've realized is that chasing every new release isn't sustainable, nor is it the most effective path to becoming a robust developer. The real power lies in grounding yourself in fundamental principles. Technologies change, but core concepts often remain surprisingly consistent.

Instead of stretching yourself thin, try this approach:
→ **Deep Dive, Don't Dabble:** Pick one modern stack (e.g., React/Node.js for web, Python/TensorFlow for ML) and commit to understanding it deeply. Build multiple projects with it.
→ **Master the 'Why':** Don't just learn syntax. Understand *why* certain patterns exist, *why* a particular architecture is chosen, and the underlying computer science principles at play. This makes adapting to new tools much easier.
→ **Problem-Solve First:** Focus on building solutions to real-world problems. The tools you use will naturally become proficient as you overcome challenges, rather than learning tools in isolation.
→ **Embrace the Learning Mindset:** The goal isn't to know everything, but to become exceptionally good at *learning anything*. Debugging skills, reading documentation, and understanding API contracts are invaluable.

This disciplined approach allows you to build a sturdy foundation. It's about becoming an adaptable engineer, not just a user of specific frameworks.

author: Afshan Ali
text:
The AI hiring wave isn't just about hiring. It's about transformation. 
 
One trend is clear: the most sought after AI talent often comes from within organizations rather than outside. We are seeing professionals shift from: 
• Data Scientist to Model Operations Engineer 
• Data Engineer to Applied AI Engineer 
• Cloud Engineer to Platform Engineer 
• AI/ML Engineer to AI Agent Developer 
 
The message is straightforward: the future belongs to those who keep improving their skills. 
For professionals with 4 to 12 years of experience, this is one of the best opportunities in years to reinvent themselves. Technical experience paired with AI skills is becoming the new standard. 
 
For recruiters, talent leaders, and GCCs, the challenge is no longer just attracting talent. It's about enabling internal movement and investing in ongoing training. 
 
The AI revolution is not replacing talent, it's changing careers. 
 
The key question is not whether AI will alter your role. It’s whether you are preparing for the role AI is creating.

author: Emil van de Streek
text:
An average AI query uses about 30 ml of water, while a single piece of steak requires 4,663 litres. 🥩

That comparison is the whole argument in this article by Ana Lúcia Castro, Devoteam Product Owner. The internet circulates numbers about AI's water footprint, and the figures tell a slightly different story.

Ana breaks down where that water actually goes (data centre cooling, the electricity generation behind it, the difference between Scope 1 and Scope 2 consumption) and stacks it against things nobody thinks twice about.

A one-hour Zoom call costs more water than 50 AI prompts. Ten minutes of 4K video costs more than a full day of typical AI use.

It's not an argument that AI is water-free. Data centres are real infrastructure with a real footprint, and the piece covers what AWS, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA are each doing to engineer that down.

But the framing matters. If you're worried about your water footprint, the shower is a better place to start than the search bar.

🔗 Read the full article in Devoteam's Magazine: https://lnkd.in/dDn-tv6M"

author: Anne Cheng
text:
The build-buy-borrow talent decision in enterprise AI is not a HR question. It is a programme design decision that determines whether your programme delivers on time.

AI talent in financial services is: scarce, expensive, competitive, and frequently drawn to organisations with the most interesting technical problems.

The talent strategy determines programme velocity.

ROLES THAT SHOULD ALMOST ALWAYS BE PERMANENT HIRES:
CoE Director and AI Governance Lead: regulatory credibility and institutional knowledge cannot be rented. These individuals will be in regulatory conversations and board presentations. They need skin in the game.

ROLES WHERE A HYBRID APPROACH MAKES SENSE:
Senior ML Engineering: 2 or 3 permanent hires for institutional knowledge; the remainder contracted or through a managed service in Year 1 while the platform stabilises.

ROLES WHERE MANAGED SERVICE OR CONTRACT MAKES SENSE IN YEAR 1:
 MLOps Engineering: the tooling decisions are not made yet. Committing to permanent MLOps headcount before the platform architecture is confirmed is a common and expensive mistake.

ROLES WHERE INTERNAL PIPELINE INVESTMENT PAYS OFF:
Data Scientists and AI Practitioners: graduate pipeline programmes take 18-24 months to yield returns but produce talent with deep institutional knowledge and lower attrition.
 
THE COMPENSATION REALITY (fully loaded, annual):
CoE Director: £250,000-400,000
Senior ML Engineer: £140,000-200,000 permanent; £900-1,400/day contract
Data Scientist: £80,000-130,000 permanent; £600-1,000/day contract
AI Product Manager: £90,000-140,000

Underfunding AI talent is not a cost saving. It is a delay, measured in months of delivery risk and the compounding cost of key person dependency on contractors who can leave.

What is the biggest talent challenge in your AI programme right now - hire, retain, or build capability? I'd like to hear where the bottleneck actually sits.

author: Lawrence Omolo
text:
The World signal appeared 16.5 hours before the mainstream press picked it up. Most pipelines registered nothing during that window. 

What does this mean for your models? It suggests a critical gap in how signals are captured and processed, particularly in relation to early language coverage. In this instance, the French press led the conversation, while other sources were yet to file their reports. As ML engineers, we understand that timing is crucial. If your pipeline isn't tuned to leverage early language signals, you may be missing pivotal moments that could shape sentiment analysis and decision-making.

This finding underscores the importance of a cohort-separated pipeline versus a merged one. While a merged pipeline might dilute these early signals, a cohort-separated approach can catch anomalies that highlight significant sentiment shifts. In this case, the sentiment around the World topic surged to 197% above its 7-day average, driven by early language coverage that mainstream sources had not yet acknowledged. The semantic gap — with terms like "world" and "cup" emerging in early discourse — contrasted sharply with the more general coverage of "Argentina," "fans," and "celebrate" in later reports.

Our API surfaces this gap. pulsebit.lojenterprise.com

author: Kopal Dixit
text:
Meta paid ₹2,400 crore (~$300M) to lock down two AI leaders.
Ruoming Pang — poached from Apple with a ~$200M package to lead AI infra at Meta's Superintelligence Labs.
Trapit Bansal — poached from OpenAI, IITian, reasoning-models specialist.
Seven months later, Pang left. For OpenAI.
Let that sink in: the single largest pay package the AI industry has ever seen... didn't buy loyalty. It bought seven months.
Here's the part that actually matters for the rest of us:
Money can buy a signature. It can't buy conviction, mission-fit, or the reason someone gets out of bed to solve a problem. @Meta just ran the most expensive experiment in the industry to prove that — and the market is still absorbing the lesson.
So what should you actually take from this?
→ Chasing the biggest paycheck without checking mission-fit is how you become a 7-month case study.
→ The real scarcity in AI right now isn't "people who can train models" — it's people who can make AI systems reliable, secure, and trustworthy in production. That skill doesn't get poached and re-poached in a talent bidding war.
→ If you're early or mid-career: don't wait for a $300M offer to matter. Build depth in AI security, applied ML ops, or agentic system design — that's where demand is compounding quietly, without the headlines.
Roles worth targeting right now: AI Security Engineer, ML Infrastructure Engineer, AI Governance/Risk Analyst, Applied AI Engineer.
Start small: one real POC, one skill you go deep on, one problem you actually care about solving.
The ₹2,400 crore headline will fade. The skill gap it's pointing at won't.

author: Gus Iwanaga
text:
A new role is taking shape in the Bay Area, still the world's innovation hub. The leading-edge companies out there are already reshaping who builds software, and Marc Andreessen just put a name to it.

"𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺'𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘪𝘳𝘤𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥 𝘢 𝘫𝘰𝘣 𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘭𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘰𝘴𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘥 '𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘥𝘦𝘳'... The product manager can generate code and design now, and each of them can do the job of all three. The idea is the jobs change so now the job is builder." He calls the current state a "three-way Mexican standoff": coders, PMs, and designers, each convinced AI means they no longer need the other two.

He's right that the walls are collapsing. I'd go further.

At commercetools, we didn't wait for the Valley to name the role. We started hiring #ProductBuilders. Based on my research, no other company in Europe had done it - we were potentially the first. I'm happy to have ignited the transformation, hiring Matea as the company's first Product Builder - she's a legend btw!

Now here's my twist. I see two roles worth building around today:
 𝟭. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿: owns product and UX, and codes right up to the engineering line.
 𝟮. 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿: because the craft of software engineering isn't going anywhere anytime soon. Front-end, back-end, full-stack, at times even the adjacent data and ML work - they all collapse into one thing now: engineers who build with AI (AKA AI engineers).

I could see most companies stoping here. I'm not.

My personal mission with my team is to take both and grow them into something bigger: the 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹-𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 (𝗙𝗦𝗣).

An FSP owns the whole arc. Conceives the idea. Does the product work. Designs the UX/UI. Writes the code. Takes it to market. It goes without saying that this whole lifecycle is done/supercharged/automated/[you-name-it] with AI.

Sounds unreasonable (lol). Good. I won't settle for less!

I break down the full thinking in a video - dropping it in the comments. 👇

author: Mouad Fettachi
text:
The biggest lesson I've learned while building in AI:
Most conversations start with "How can we improve model accuracy?"

But after talking to ML engineers and AI teams, I've realized that's often the wrong place to start.

The real questions are:
-->Can you trust your labels?
-->Is your data consistent?
-->How much engineering time is spent moving datasets between different tools?
-->How many "model problems" are actually data problems?

I've seen teams spend days experimenting with new models when the issue was buried much earlier in the pipeline.

A better model can't fix inconsistent data.
It can't fix noisy annotations.
And it definitely can't fix a messy workflow.

The more I learn, the more I believe AI isn't limited by models.
It's limited by how efficiently we prepare and manage data.

That's one of the reasons we're building LabelBricks.

Not because the world needs another annotation tool.

But because the data layer still feels far more fragmented than it should.

Curious to hear from people working in ML:
What's been the biggest bottleneck in your workflow recently?

🎯 Can you survive an AI interviewer? Most people can't get past Level 2.

I built AI Interview Coach — it speaks interview questions out loud 🗣️, listens to your spoken answers 🎙️, and scores you like a real interviewer.

Try it free here:
https://lnkd.in/dyTnzZDt

Pick any topic — Python, SQL, System Design, ML, React, DevOps — and face a strict, realistic interview:

✅ AI-generated questions that escalate: easy → intermediate → advanced → expert
✅ It reads every question aloud, just like a phone-screen interviewer
✅ Answer by voice — it transcribes as you speak (typing works too)
✅ Every answer scored 0–5 with brutally honest feedback
✅ Score 60% to unlock the next level — fail and you stay put 😅
✅ Final readiness report telling you if you're actually job-ready

🏆 Challenge: take one interview and comment your highest level + topic below. Let's see who reaches Expert first.

⚙️ For the engineers and hiring managers — the AI engineering I implemented end-to-end:

1. LLM Orchestration — Groq (Llama 3.3 70B) primary with automatic Gemini failover; one provider failing never kills an interview
2. RAG — ChromaDB + MiniLM embeddings ground the evaluation against a curated Q&A corpus, with a lightweight keyword-retrieval fallback engineered for serverless limits
3. Voice AI — hands-free loop: text-to-speech questions + speech-to-text answers
4. MCP (Model Context Protocol) — a server exposing interview tools so AI assistants like Claude can drive the platform directly
5. Prompt engineering — difficulty-calibrated question generation + strict rubric scoring that resists gibberish answers
6. Serverless architecture — stateless design, browser owns session state, zero pip dependencies on Vercel
7. Auth from scratch — PBKDF2 hashing + HMAC-signed tokens in pure Python stdlib, with role-based access (owner/admin/user)
8. Analytics dashboard — per-user interview history, topic trends, level distribution, live usage metrics

💡 Hardest lesson: Vercel's size limit killed my 200MB vector stack. Rebuilding retrieval within constraints made the app faster. Constraints > resources.

These are exactly the skills I want to bring to my next AI Engineering role — if your team builds with LLMs, RAG, voice AI, or agentic systems, my DMs are open 📬

That's no longer science fiction. AutoML lets algorithms automatically search through thousands of possible models and pick the best one for the task, no ML PhD required. In medicine, that means the clinician defines the question and the machine engineers the solution.
In this new study we put it to the test: 11 AutoML frameworks, 10 imaging datasets across CT and MRI, multiple anatomies and clinical endpoints. The result is a clear signal that self-optimizing AI is ready to democratize radiomics.
The next frontier is end-to-end, image-to-prediction workflows that require no code at all. That's the direction we're building toward. Proud of this team. 👇

author: Petr Blabolil
text:
An average AI query uses about 30 ml of water, while a single piece of steak requires 4,663 litres. 🥩

That comparison is the whole argument in this article by Ana Lúcia Castro, Devoteam Product Owner. The internet circulates numbers about AI's water footprint, and the figures tell a slightly different story.

Ana breaks down where that water actually goes (data centre cooling, the electricity generation behind it, the difference between Scope 1 and Scope 2 consumption) and stacks it against things nobody thinks twice about.

A one-hour Zoom call costs more water than 50 AI prompts. Ten minutes of 4K video costs more than a full day of typical AI use.

It's not an argument that AI is water-free. Data centres are real infrastructure with a real footprint, and the piece covers what AWS, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA are each doing to engineer that down.

But the framing matters. If you're worried about your water footprint, the shower is a better place to start than the search bar.

text:
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝗧𝗦 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗟𝗼𝘄 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆

Writing technical content for developers and ML engineers requires more than just good ideas. It requires precision. If you mix opinions with unsupported numbers, you lose trust.

Use these controls to verify your content before you publish.

The Three Layer Rule

A good article separates three distinct layers:

- Facts: Rules, statistics, or documented constraints.
- Estimates: Conservative orders of magnitude.
- Choices: How an operator acts during uncertainty.

Do not blend these layers. If you mix a fact with an opinion in one sentence, you weaken your authority.

The Source Framework

Assign one specific job to every source you use. This prevents articles that cite many things but prove nothing.

- Official Sources: Use these to define rules or boundaries.
- Research Sources: Use these to support trends or measurements.
- Consulting Sources: Use these to interpret business impact like risk or cost.

The Pre-Publication Checklist

Before you hit publish, answer these five questions:

- Angle: What decision can the reader make after reading this?
- Official Source: Does a public authority frame this topic?
- Data: Is the statistical range defensible?
- Consulting View: Is the business impact tied to risk or priority?
- Internal Links: Does the link help the reader or just push a domain?

If a row in your checklist stays empty, your article lacks evidence. It is better to miss a publication day than to publish a weak signal.

Honesty builds long-term value. A piece that admits its limits can be updated. A piece that overstates certainty becomes useless when data changes.

text:
Inside an AI Readiness Assessment
What's Inside an AI Readiness Assessment? (The Complete Framework)
 After 50+ assessments, we've narrowed AI readiness to 4 critical pillars.
 
Here's what we evaluate—and why it matters:
 
Pillar 1: Skills & Organization (20% of score)
What We Assess:
 - Does your organization have an AI sponsor/champion?
 - Do you have data scientists, data engineers, ML ops people?
 - Do non-technical teams understand LLMs?
 - Is there budget allocated for training?
 
 Why It Matters:
 AI systems don't run themselves. You need someone who owns the strategy, maintains models, and troubleshoots issues.
 What We Deliver:
 - Skills gap analysis
 - Recommended hiring profile
 - Training roadmap
 Pillar 2: Data Readiness (30% of score)
 
What We Assess:
 - Where does your data live? (ERP, CRM, legacy, unstructured?)
 - Is data documented/cataloged?
 - What's the data quality? (Completeness, accuracy, consistency)
 - Do you have access governance?
 - Can you integrate data sources?
 
Why It Matters:
Garbage in = garbage out. Poor data quality means LLM models will give poor results, no matter how advanced the model is.
 
 What We Deliver:
 - Data inventory + quality scoring
 - Integration roadmap
 - Data governance recommendations
 Pillar 3: Infrastructure & Security (25% of score)

What We Assess:
 - Can your systems integrate with APIs?
 - Where can data be deployed? (On-prem, cloud, regional cloud?)
 - What's your security/encryption posture?
 - Can you scale compute as needed?
 - Are there audit/logging capabilities?
 
Why It Matters:
Modern AI needs modern infrastructure. Legacy systems create bottlenecks. Poor security = compliance violations + data breaches.
 
What We Deliver:
 - Infrastructure readiness report
 - Cloud strategy recommendation
 - Security compliance gap analysis
 Pillar 4: Regulatory & Compliance (25% of score)
What We Assess:
 - What regulations apply to your industry/data? (PDPL, SAMA, NCA, etc.)
 - Do you have data residency requirements?
 - Are there consent/transparency requirements?
 - Can you audit AI decisions?
 - What's your data retention policy?
 
Why It Matters:
Non-compliance = legal risk, fines, reputational damage. An AI system that violates PDPL or SAMA is worse than no AI at all.
 
What We Deliver:
 - Regulatory gap analysis
 - Compliance roadmap
 - Architecture recommendations (on-prem vs. cloud)
 
 The Output:
 A comprehensive AI Readiness Score (0–100):
 
 - 80–100: Ready for enterprise AI. Proceed with confidence.
 - 60–79: Ready with caveats. Address 2–3 gaps first.
 - 40–59: Significant gaps. Need 3–6 months of foundation work.
 - <40: Not ready. Recommend Phase 0 work before attempting AI.
 
Plus: Prioritized roadmap addressing the biggest gaps first.

Typical Finding:
Most enterprises score 50–65 out of 100. Not bad, but not ready. 
That's actually good news—because it means the assessment reveals what to fix before you invest.

text:
A friend of mine just did something I didn't think was possible and it made me rethink everything about "career switches."

She spent close to 8 years in a completely non-tech field. No coding background, no CS degree, nothing IT-related on her resume.
A year ago, she decided she wanted in specifically into the AI/ML space, which honestly sounded even more ambitious given where she was starting from.
I asked her last week what actually worked, because so many people talk about "upskilling" without ever explaining how. Here's what she told me:
She didn't try to learn everything at once. She picked one lane prompt engineering and AI-assisted workflows instead of drowning in Python, ML theory, and cloud all together
She used GenAI tools daily, not just to learn concepts, but to simulate real work writing prompts for actual business problems, debugging her own logic, building small AI-powered tools
She built a portfolio of practical projects instead of collecting certificates things like automating a workflow with AI, building a simple chatbot, analyzing data with AI assistance stuff she could actually show, not just talk about
She used AI to rewrite her resume and LinkedIn from a "non-tech" narrative to one that highlighted transferable skills problem-solving, communication, domain expertise framed for AI-adjacent roles
She practiced explaining her projects out loud with AI as her mock interviewer, until she stopped sounding like she was apologizing for her background
What stuck with me most was something she said:
"I stopped trying to prove I could code like an engineer. I focused on proving I could think with AI that's what these roles actually need right now."
She's now working in an AI-focused role, less than a year after starting from zero.
If you're on the fence about switching into tech because you think you're "too non-technical" her story is proof that the entry point has changed. You don't need a CS degree anymore. You need curiosity, consistency, and the willingness to actually use these tools instead of just reading about them.

author: Pedro Lourenco
text:
Most people learn mechanistic interpretability backwards.
They start with sparse autoencoders because that is the flashy bit...

Then they wonder why a list of labelled features still does not explain the computation.

Mechanistic interpretability is not attention heatmaps.
It is the attempt to reverse-engineer the causal algorithms a model has learned.

Here’s the exact path, in order.
Math and ML foundations: understand vectors, matrices, gradients and PyTorch well enough to manipulate activations rather than merely inspect outputs.

Transformer anatomy: learn embeddings, the residual stream, QK and OV circuits, attention heads, MLPs, layer normalisation and unembedding.

Read model internals: use hooks, activation caches, the logit lens, direct logit attribution and weight analysis to form hypotheses.

Causal interventions: test those hypotheses with ablations, activation patching, path patching and carefully chosen metrics. Correlation is not a mechanism.

Circuit discovery: reproduce induction heads and the IOI circuit. This is where isolated components become an algorithm implemented across layers.

Feature dictionaries: study superposition, polysemanticity, sparse autoencoders and transcoders. These methods change the unit of analysis from neurons to learned features.

Attribution graphs: trace feature-to-feature computation at scale, then validate the graph for faithfulness, sufficiency and completeness. The frontier is automated model biology, not prettier dashboards.

Save this if you want to start learning about mech. interp. but don't know where to start. 

Follow for the next Mastery Path.

author: Ghulam Mustafa Khoso
text:
For the longest time, I thought learning Machine Learning meant understanding every mathematical proof before writing a single line of code.

I spent hours watching tutorials, jumping between playlists, and trying to memorize formulas. The result? Lots of theory, very little confidence.

Recently, I changed my learning approach.

Instead of asking, "Can I derive every equation?", I started asking, "How would an AI/ML engineer solve this problem in the real world?"

Today, I completed a practical Logistic Regression project using a healthcare dataset to predict whether a patient is likely to have a disease based on clinical and lifestyle features such as:
• Age
• Gender
• Blood Glucose
• Cholesterol
• Blood Pressure
• BMI
• Heart Rate
• Smoking & Alcohol Habits
• Physical Activity
• Family History

Rather than focusing only on the algorithm, I followed an end-to-end industry workflow:

✅ Understanding the business problem
✅ Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
✅ Data cleaning & preprocessing
✅ Feature engineering
✅ Train–test split
✅ Feature scaling
✅ Training a Logistic Regression model
✅ Class prediction & probability prediction
✅ Evaluating with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, ROC-AUC & Confusion Matrix
✅ Understanding where the model succeeds—and where it makes mistakes

One insight stood out:

Building a machine learning model is much more than calling model.fit(). Most of the engineering effort goes into understanding the data, preparing meaningful features, and evaluating the model with the right metrics.

To reinforce this learning, I also created a complete Classification Pipeline Blueprint that documents the workflow from raw data to a production-ready model. My goal is to build a practical collection of AI/ML engineering pipelines that beginners can follow without getting overwhelmed by endless tutorials.

This is another step in my journey toward becoming a professional AI/ML Engineer. Every project teaches me something new, and I'm excited to keep learning, building, and sharing.

I'd love to hear from experienced ML engineers:

What's one lesson you wish you had learned earlier when working with classification models?
